assumptions: The target buyer is a central finance, controllership, or compliance team at a multi-store Polish retailer with genuinely heterogeneous operator, POS, RVM, and accounting paths, rather than an individual store.
The initial service can operate from retailer-authorized read-only exports without taking custody of deposits, acting as a statutory operator, or requiring continuous production integrations.
No supplied evidence establishes that essential data rights are unobtainable, but commercially usable access, identifier quality, and derived-data reuse rights remain unresolved.

The advertised incumbent price band is a relevant ceiling for routine operational software, while a chain-level independent audit could command a higher fee only if it documents recoveries or material close-effort savings.

The founder keeps the corporate job during validation, contributes roughly 12-16 hours per week, and uses contractors selectively for security or connector work within the stated 70000 PLN initial-capital envelope.
The supplied research is the complete evidence set for this evaluation; absent pilot, buyer, partner, and private variance data are treated as uncertainty rather than proof of failure.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: Results from at least three heterogeneous multi-store chains showing the post-incumbent variance rate and PLN value, recovery and false-positive rates, finance hours saved, lawful export availability, onboarding and connector cost, a named budget owner paying a value-based fee, repeat monitoring demand, and an acquisition path with credible CAC and payback.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: The law-created combination of monthly settlement, detailed retailer records, and multiple operators makes cross-system mismatches plausible, and an independent evidence-linked exception layer is more coherent than another primary DRS ledger. The insight is constrained by the lack of evidence that a material unexplained exception pool survives the verification and reports already supplied by operators, COMP, and POS vendors.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Deposit close and recordkeeping recur and can affect cash and finance labor, so a recoverable discrepancy would be an economically legible pain. However, no evidence quantifies unresolved losses, close effort, buyer urgency, or separate willingness to pay after incumbent reconciliation, while existing tooling already addresses much of the visible operational burden at low prices.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: A bounded historical audit can be sold before building a full platform and could have attractive software-assisted gross margin if recoveries are large. The proposed 20-80 PLN per-location subscription sits inside the incumbent price band, yet the product may require expensive bespoke connectors, secure data handling, analyst review, support, and enterprise procurement; CAC, integration cost, retention, LTV, payback, and realistic owner earnings are all unmeasured, and the supplied record does not evidence the founder-net-worth path.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Multi-store grocery, franchise, and wholesale groups above 200 square metres with heterogeneous system paths form an identifiable and operationally coherent beachhead, and national return volume is already large. The economically relevant subset is much narrower than total return points, because the opportunity depends on chains that have both cross-system complexity and material residual variances; its count and spend pool are unknown.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Independence across operators and retailer systems could create a useful neutral-control position. Nevertheless, COMP, PolKa, Insoft, and other embedded providers already possess integrations, settlement workflows, customer relationships, and data access, and they can add exception analytics more easily than a new entrant can displace their channel position; no exclusive access or segment-control mechanism is established.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A proven reconciliation engine and exception taxonomy could extend across retailer formats, operators, adjacent finance controls, and eventually other deposit-system geographies. Those adjacencies become valuable only after the Polish wedge proves access, repeatable recoveries, and portable identifiers, and different contracts and national rules may limit transferability.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Permissioned mappings of exception causes and successful resolution packets could improve automation over time and create some workflow switching cost. Data-reuse rights are unresolved, early mappings are reproducible, and incumbents have superior raw-data access and installed distribution, so the proposed learning asset is neither assured nor protected from rapid imitation.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: The offer could be more neutral and more finance-control-oriented than an operator's or POS vendor's own report, especially when it links a discrepancy to an operator-ready evidence packet. There is no measured recovery rate, false-positive rate, close-time reduction, or coverage advantage showing that this distinction is large enough to change purchasing behavior.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: The mandated system is operating at large scale, eight operators create structural complexity, and recently established processes may still expose reconciliation gaps, making a targeted audit timely. The same rapid deployment also shows that core infrastructure and major relationships are already in place, so the entry window may narrow as incumbents improve controls.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: A one-month audit gives a concrete entry offer, central finance teams are identifiable, and accounting or technology partners could concentrate access to chains. No named buyer or partner commitment supports this route, enterprise trust and security reviews can lengthen sales, and the most attractive POS and DRS partners may prefer their own analytics or restrict access, leaving repeatable CAC and payback unknown.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: Read-only auditing avoids deposit custody and fits the founder's data-science and automation strengths; one export-based pilot is plausible part-time with controlled capital. Reliable entity matching across heterogeneous systems, contractual permission, information security, false-positive control, enterprise selling, and ongoing connector maintenance are substantial, and several depend on counterparties rather than AI-assisted implementation alone.

highest_value_structural_change: Make the entry business an accounting-partner-distributed, outcome-priced closed-month recovery audit using customer-authorized file exports, with a meaningful minimum fee plus a share of verified recovery or savings; defer low-price per-store SaaS and bespoke production connectors until repeated audits prove a large recurring exception class that can be standardized.
main_structural_strength: A bounded, read-only historical recovery audit can isolate a neutral finance-control wedge from the already commoditized operational DRS stack, align fees with provable cash or labor value, and be tested before continuous integrations or regulated fund handling.
primary_score_limiter: The opportunity has not established that post-incumbent residual variances are frequent and valuable enough to fund heterogeneous data access and integration; low incumbent pricing and incumbent control of both data and channels reinforce this uncertainty across economics, advantage, and distribution.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: COMP already markets multi-operator settlement visibility, reports, integrations, and 19.90-79.90 PLN monthly retailer tiers, while PolKa verifies the quantities and values used for settlement and Insoft embeds settlement reporting in an established POS product; this directly weakens the premise that retailers retain a separately monetizable reconciliation gap.
